The S-Tier Answer: Design a Notification System

"Design a notification system" is one of the most common system design questions, and one of the easiest to answer badly.

Here are four answers I hear, ranked:

This page is the full S-tier answer, step by step, the way I would actually run it in a 45-minute round. Each sub-problem gets its own diagram.

The running example is a food delivery app like Zomato or Swiggy, because it has every kind of notification in one product: OTPs, order updates, and a sale message to every user at 7 PM.

Step 1: Clarify before you draw anything

The S-tier answer starts exactly where the A-tier answer starts: with questions. The difference is that every answer turns into a design decision.

QuestionAnswer for this appWhat it changes in the design
What kinds of notifications?OTPs, order updates, promotionsTwo different systems hiding behind one name
Can we lose some?OTPs and order updates: never. Promotions: occasionally, yesDurability only where it is needed
How fast?OTP within seconds. Order updates within seconds. A sale can take minutesSeparate lanes and priorities
Which channels?Push, SMS, emailOne pipeline, pluggable channel adapters
Do we need ordering?Per order: "delivered" must never arrive before "out for delivery"Order per key, not globally
What if a provider is down?OTP must still arriveFallback provider for critical messages
What should never be retried?An expired OTP, a sale that has ended, an invalid device tokenExpiry on every message, error classification
Who can opt out?Promotions: anyone, any time. Transactional: noPreferences apply to one lane only

If you only take one thing from this page, take this table. Everything below is these answers turned into boxes.

Step 2: Functional requirements

  1. Other services can send a notification to a user: an OTP, an order update, a payment receipt.
  2. The marketing team can send a campaign to a segment of users, or to everyone.
  3. Users can choose which categories they receive on which channel, and set quiet hours.
  4. Each notification goes out on push, SMS or email, with a fallback channel for critical ones.
  5. Anyone can see the status of a notification: queued, sent, delivered, failed.
  6. Devices register and refresh their push tokens.

Out of scope for this round: building our own push network (we use FCM for Android and APNs for iOS), in-app inbox UI, and the content of the messages themselves.

Step 3: Non-functional requirements

Transactional lane (OTP, order updates)Promotional lane (campaigns)
DurabilityNever lost once the order is committedBest effort; a few lost is acceptable
LatencySeconds, end to endMinutes is fine
DeliveryAt least once, deduplicated so the user sees it onceAt most once per user per campaign
OrderingPer orderNot needed
ExpiryOTP expires with the code; order updates expire when the order closesExpires when the sale ends
IsolationA campaign must never slow down an OTPUses only the capacity the transactional lane is not using
Respect preferencesNo (you cannot opt out of your OTP)Yes, plus quiet hours and frequency caps

Two more that apply to both: the send API stays available even when a provider is down, and every stage is observable, because "the notification never arrived" is the most common support ticket this system will get.

Step 4: Back-of-the-envelope numbers

These are assumptions for a large Indian food delivery app. Say them out loud in the interview; the exact values matter less than the shape.

  • Users: 50 million devices with a push token.
  • Orders: 5 million orders a day, each with about 4 updates (placed, accepted, out for delivery, delivered), so about 20 million transactional notifications a day. That is about 230 per second on average, and maybe 5x that at dinner time: about 1,200 per second at peak.
  • OTPs: say 2 million a day, about 25 per second, peaking in the low hundreds.
  • A campaign to everyone: 50 million messages. Sent over 5 minutes, that is about 170,000 per second. Over 20 minutes, about 42,000 per second.
  • The part people miss: if even 5% of 50 million people open the app within a minute of the sale message, that is 2.5 million people hitting search, menus and checkout at once.
  • Storage: transactional records at about 1 KB each are about 20 GB a day; 30 days hot is about 600 GB. For a campaign, store the campaign once plus compact per-user delivery status, not 50 million full copies of the message.

What the numbers say: the transactional lane is small and must be perfect. The promotional lane is huge and bursty. And the real danger is not sending the sale, it is surviving the response to it. That is the bottleneck.

Step 5: API

These are internal APIs; other services call them, users never do.

Send one notification (transactional):

POST /v1/notifications
Idempotency-Key: order-o_789-out-for-delivery

{
  "user_id": "u_123",
  "category": "order_update",
  "template": "order_out_for_delivery",
  "data": { "order_id": "o_789", "eta_min": 12 },
  "priority": "high",
  "channels": ["push", "sms"],
  "expires_at": "2026-10-28T20:30:00+05:30"
}

202 Accepted
{ "notification_id": "n_456", "status": "queued" }

The Idempotency-Key is not decoration. The caller will retry, and the same key must never produce two notifications.

Start a campaign (promotional):

POST /v1/campaigns

{
  "name": "diwali-sale-7pm",
  "audience": { "segment": "active_last_30_days" },
  "template": "sale_live",
  "send_window": { "start": "2026-10-28T19:00:00+05:30", "spread_minutes": 15 },
  "expires_at": "2026-10-28T23:59:00+05:30",
  "priority": "low"
}

202 Accepted
{ "campaign_id": "c_42", "status": "scheduled" }

The rest:

  • GET /v1/notifications/{id}: status and the attempt history
  • POST /v1/devices and DELETE /v1/devices/{device_id}: register or remove a push token
  • PUT /v1/users/{id}/preferences: categories per channel, quiet hours, time zone

Step 6: Data model

TableKey fieldsWhy it exists
outbox (in the order service's own database)id, order_id, event_type, payload, created_at, published_atMakes "order saved" and "notification promised" one atomic write (deep dive 1)
notificationsnotification_id, user_id, idempotency_key (unique), category, priority, payload, status, expires_atOne row per transactional notification
delivery_attemptsnotification_id, channel, provider, attempt, result, error_code, atDebugging "it never arrived"
devicesuser_id, device_id, platform, push_token, last_seen_at, validWhere to send; invalid tokens get removed
preferencesuser_id, per-category channel settings, quiet hours, time zoneFilters for the promotional lane
campaignscampaign_id, audience, template, send_window, expires_at, status, countersOne row per campaign, not per user

At 20 million rows a day, a relational database partitioned by day is enough for the transactional tables. Do not reach for a new database just because the word "scale" appeared in the question.

Step 7: High-level design

Two lanes that share the last mile:

  • Transactional lane. The order service writes the order and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay publishes outbox rows to the notification service, which deduplicates, renders the template, and puts the message on the high-priority queue.
  • Promotional lane. The campaign service resolves the audience, applies preferences, plans the fan-out in waves, and feeds the low-priority queue at a controlled rate.
  • Shared last mile. Channel workers (push, SMS, email) take high priority first, call the providers through adapters, and write every result to the status store. Provider feedback, like "this token is no longer registered", flows back to clean up devices.

Now the deep dives. This is where the round is decided.

Deep dive 1: Never lose an OTP or an order update

The tempting design is: save the order, then call the notification service.

That is two writes to two systems. If the process crashes between them, the order exists and the notification is gone forever. Retrying in the same process does not help, because the process is the thing that died.

The fix is the transactional outbox:

  1. In the same database transaction as the order, insert a row into an outbox table: "send out-for-delivery for order o_789".
  2. Commit. Now the order and the promise to notify are one atomic fact. Either both exist or neither does.
  3. A relay reads unpublished outbox rows (by polling, or by reading the database's change log), publishes them, and marks them published.

If the relay crashes, it simply reads the same rows again when it comes back. Nothing is lost. That gives us at-least-once delivery, which brings the next problem.

Deep dive 2: At least once, but the user sees it once

At-least-once means duplicates. The relay may publish a row twice. A worker may send to FCM and crash before recording success, so the message is picked up again.

  • Every notification carries an idempotency key derived from the business event (order-o_789-out-for-delivery), not a random ID generated at send time.
  • The notifications table has a unique constraint on that key, so a second insert of the same event is a no-op.
  • Before calling a provider, the worker checks and records the attempt for (notification_id, channel). A redelivered message whose send already succeeded is acknowledged and skipped.
  • For ordering, partition the queue by order_id, so one order's updates are processed in sequence, and carry a sequence number so a late "out for delivery" never overwrites "delivered" on the user's screen.

You cannot get exactly-once delivery across a network. You can get at-least-once delivery plus idempotency, which looks exactly-once to the user.

Deep dive 3: Two lanes, so a sale never delays an OTP

If OTPs and the 7 PM sale share one queue, the OTP waits behind 50 million sale messages. Your users cannot log in during your biggest sale.

  • Separate queues for high and low priority. Workers always drain high priority first.
  • Separate worker pools, so a slow campaign cannot occupy every worker.
  • Reserved provider capacity. Providers rate-limit you. Reserve a share of the quota for the transactional lane, and let campaigns use only what is left. A token bucket per provider, with the high-priority lane allowed to borrow from the low-priority one and never the other way round.

This is the "can we lose some of them?" question turned into architecture: the lane you cannot lose gets the guarantees, and the lane you can lose gets the volume.

Deep dive 4: Fan-out for 50 million users

There are two very different cases, and the S-tier answer names both.

Broadcast (same message for everyone). Subscribe devices to a topic like india_sale_users and send one message to the topic. FCM does the fan-out to every subscribed device on its side. One API call instead of 50 million. This is the cheapest and simplest option, so start here.

The tradeoff: a topic is coarse. Everyone subscribed gets the message at roughly the same time, and you cannot apply per-user quiet hours or frequency caps inside one topic send. You can split the audience into several topics (by city, by wave) to get some control back.

Personalised (different offer per user, or per-user rules). Now you send per device:

  1. The campaign service writes one event: "campaign c_42 started".
  2. A planner splits the audience into partitions, by user ID range or by city.
  3. Many workers each take a partition, fetch device tokens in chunks, apply preferences and caps, render, and send through the rate limiter.
  4. Each worker records success and failure counts, retries temporary failures, and removes invalid tokens.

No machine ever loops over 50 million users. Thousands of small jobs make progress independently, and a crashed worker only redoes its own partition.

Deep dive 5: Don't DDoS your own backend

This is the bottleneck from step 4, and the part most answers miss.

Suppose delivery works perfectly and 50 million phones buzz at exactly 7:00 PM. If 5% open the app in the first minute, 2.5 million people hit search, menus, offers and checkout together. Your notification system worked so well that it took down your own app.

So the S-tier design spreads delivery on purpose:

  • Send in waves over 10 to 20 minutes. The sale still feels simultaneous to users.
  • Send the high-intent users first (ordered recently, opened the app this week), so the first wave converts while capacity is fresh.
  • Size each wave from the backend's capacity, not from how fast the providers can send.
  • Watch app traffic during the campaign and slow the remaining waves automatically if latency or error rates climb.

A promo that arrives four minutes late costs nothing. An app that falls over at 7 PM costs the whole sale.

Deep dive 6: What to retry, and what never to retry

"Add retries" is a B-tier answer. The S-tier answer classifies every failure.

Result from the providerExampleWhat to do
Temporary failureFCM UNAVAILABLE or INTERNAL, an HTTP 5xxRetry with exponential backoff and jitter
Rate limitedFCM QUOTA_EXCEEDED, HTTP 429Back off, honour Retry-After, slow the lane down
Token is deadFCM UNREGISTERED, APNs 410Never retry. Mark the token invalid and stop sending to it
Bad requestFCM INVALID_ARGUMENTNever retry. It will fail the same way. Send to a dead-letter queue and alert
ExpiredOTP past its validity, sale already endedNever retry. Drop it. A late OTP is worse than none: the user has already asked for a new one

Two rules make this safe:

  • Every message carries expires_at, and workers check it before every attempt, including retries.
  • Retries have a budget. A fixed number of attempts and a total time limit, after which the message goes to a dead-letter queue with its error history.

Deep dive 7: When a provider goes down

Providers have outages. An OTP that cannot be delivered means a user who cannot log in.

  • Put a circuit breaker around each provider adapter. When errors or timeouts cross a threshold, the circuit opens and stops sending traffic into a provider that is failing.
  • For OTPs, keep a second SMS provider and switch to it when the first one's circuit opens. If both fail, fall back to another channel the user has, like email or a voice call.
  • For order updates, push is primary; for the few that matter most (the delivery partner is at your door), fall back to SMS if push is not confirmed.
  • For promotions, do not fail over. Pause the campaign and resume when the provider recovers, or let it expire. Paying for SMS to deliver a sale message nobody asked for urgently is a cost, not a feature.

Deep dive 8: Preferences, quiet hours and frequency caps

The promotional lane must respect the user. The transactional lane must ignore most of these rules, because you cannot opt out of your OTP.

Before any promotional send, each message passes through:

  1. Opted in? The user's preference for this category on this channel. If not, skip.
  2. Quiet hours? Using the user's own time zone. If it is 11 PM for them, defer the message to the morning, or drop it if it will have expired by then.
  3. Frequency cap? For example, at most two promotions per user per day across all campaigns. If the cap is reached, skip.
  4. Duplicate? At most one message per user per campaign.

Cache preferences close to the workers, because 50 million lookups against the main database during a campaign is its own outage.

Deep dive 9: Observability

"My OTP never came" is a ticket you will get every day. Without tracking every stage you cannot answer it.

Track the funnel per lane and per channel: requested, queued, sent to the provider, accepted by the provider, delivered (where the channel reports it), opened.

The metrics I would alert on:

  • Transactional lane lag: time from the outbox row to the provider call. This is the one that pages someone.
  • Outbox backlog: unpublished rows growing means the relay is stuck.
  • Provider error rate by code: a jump in UNREGISTERED is token churn; a jump in 5xx is an outage.
  • Retry and dead-letter volume.
  • Campaign progress against its window, and app latency during each wave.

Step 8: The simplest version I would ship first

The S-tier answer is not the biggest diagram. It is the one that knows what to build now and what to add later.

Ship firstAdd later, when the numbers demand it
Outbox table in the order database, plus one relayChange-data-capture instead of polling
One queue per lane, a small pool of workersA distributed log like Kafka, when one queue cannot keep up
Topic sends for broadcasts, in a few wavesPersonalised fan-out with a planner and partitions
Idempotency key with a unique constraintPer-provider dedupe caches
expires_at on every message, retries with a budgetSmart send-time per user
One SMS fallback provider for OTPsMulti-provider routing on cost and latency
The funnel metrics and the lag alertA full delivery analytics pipeline

No new microservice for everything. No Kafka on day one. Just the parts that keep the promises from step 1.

How to say it in the interview

When you finish, summarise in three sentences, because this is what the interviewer writes down:

  1. The bottleneck: "The hard part isn't sending 50 million messages, it's the traffic when people open the app, so I stagger the waves and size them from backend capacity."
  2. The tradeoff: "A promo can arrive late, an OTP can't. So the transactional lane gets the outbox, idempotency, priority and failover, and the promotional lane gets volume and best effort."
  3. What I'd ship first: "An outbox, two queues, topic sends in waves, expiry on every message, and the lag alert. Everything else waits for the numbers."

Titles can be hidden. Judgment cannot.
